result: {"decisions":[{"point":"D1","problem":"How to assess a defense's robustness when the space of possible poisoning attacks is near-limitless and testing known attacks cannot rule out new ones.","did":"They built a framework that computes approximate upper bounds on worst-case loss over all attacks, paired with a candidate attack, instead of only testing hypothesized attacks.","alternatives_named":["testing a defense against a number of known poisoning strategies on a clean dataset","hypothetical attacks designed to test defenses"],"stated_reason":"It is impossible to conclude from empirical success alone that a defense that works against known attacks will not fail against a new attack.","quote":"However, because of the near-limitless space of possible attacks, it is impossible to conclude from empirical success alone that a defense that works against a known set of attacks will not fail against a new attack."},{"point":"D5","problem":"The true worst-case test loss is hard to bound directly, so a tractable surrogate is needed and its validity must be interpreted.","did":"They approximated test loss by clean training loss, upper bounded it by loss on the full data, and let the defender train on all clean data, yielding a minimax loss M whose validity rests on two stated assumptions.","alternatives_named":["bilevel optimization of the worst-case test loss directly"],"stated_reason":"M admits a natural minimax formulation with duality properties that give insight into the optimal attack, whereas the direct bilevel problem is intractable in general.","quote":"The approximations (i) and (iii) define the assumptions we need for our certificates to hold; as long as both approximations are valid, $\\mathbf{M}$ will give an approximate upper bound on the worst-case test loss."},{"point":"D2","problem":"How to tell how tight the computed upper bound on the minimax loss is.","did":"They pair the upper bound with a candidate attack whose induced loss is a lower bound, and monitor the duality gap between them.","alternatives_named":[],"stated_reason":"The gap between lower and upper bounds indicates the quality of the bounds, and convexity plus sublinear regret makes the gap vanish for large datasets.","quote":"We can monitor the duality gap between lower and upper bounds on $\\mathbf{M}$ to ascertain the quality of the bounds."},{"point":"D1","problem":"Which kind of defender to analyze: one whose feasible set is independent of the poisoned data, or one estimated from the possibly poisoned data.","did":"They analyzed both fixed oracle defenses and data-dependent defenses, using the oracle as a bound on what is achievable and then testing the realistic data-dependent case.","alternatives_named":["fixed defenses","data-dependent defenses"],"stated_reason":"Oracle defenders are not implementable but provide bounds: if even an oracle can be attacked, we should be worried; data-dependent defenders are implementable but open a new line of attack.","quote":"While such defenders are not implementable in practice, they provide bounds: if even an oracle can be attacked, then we should be worried."},{"point":"D2","problem":"Whether the candidate attack from the framework is actually strong, given that existing attack methods exist.","did":"They compared their candidate attack against two baselines, gradient descent on test loss and label flipping, and also checked maximum test 0-1 error against the certificates.","alternatives_named":["gradient descent on the test loss","label flipping baseline"],"stated_reason":"Baselines provide a check that the framework's attack is strongest and that test error is consistent with the certificate; label flipping is too weak and gradient gets stuck in local minima.","quote":"Our attack consistently performs strongest; label flipping seems to be too weak, while the gradient algorithm seems to get stuck in local minima."},{"point":"D3","problem":"Whether to accept an imperfect attack and bound on text data when the integer program is too hard to solve well, leaving a large gap.","did":"They accepted a valid candidate attack from the IQP solver (or randomized rounding for IMDB) with a relaxed upper bound, noting the gap, and drew conclusions from the attack's success anyway.","alternatives_named":["solving the IQP exactly","relaxing the integrity constraints only"],"stated_reason":"The integer constraints make solving expensive and IMDB was too large for Gurobi, but the attacks were still relatively successful despite the gap.","quote":"Results are given in Figure 3; there is a relatively large gap between the upper bound and the attack. Despite this, the attacks are relatively successful."},{"point":"D5","problem":"Why the IMDB dataset is far more attackable than MNIST-1-7 under the same oracle defense.","did":"They inspected the geometry of the feasible set (Figure 1) and attributed the difference to high dimensionality and many irrelevant features enlarging the feasible set without separating the classes.","alternatives_named":[],"stated_reason":"Irrelevant features increase the size of F without a corresponding increase in class separation, so the defense places few constraints on the attacker.","quote":"This seems to be a consequence of the high dimensionality of IMDB and the large number of irrelevant features, which increase the size of $\\mathcal{F}$ without a corresponding increase in separation between the classes."},{"point":"D6","problem":"How strongly to state what the certificates guarantee, given they must be computed on clean data and rest on approximations.","did":"They framed the bounds as a design-stage assessment tool modulo approximations, explicitly not a guarantee for a deployed algorithm.","alternatives_named":["guaranteeing performance of a deployed learning algorithm"],"stated_reason":"The method needs to be run on the clean data, which presumably would not be available at deployment time.","quote":"We stress that our bounds are meant to be used as a way to assess defense strategies in the design stage, rather than guaranteeing performance of a deployed learning algorithm"}]}
